strengths: The paper tackles a useful and significant problem: one feed-forward model accepts optional depth, intrinsics, and pose priors while producing point maps, depth, camera parameters, normals, and 3D Gaussians.

The empirical breadth is impressive. Results cover reconstruction, pose estimation, normal estimation, depth, and novel-view synthesis across numerous datasets. In particular, Tables 1 and 4 report substantial gains over strong recent baselines, and the qualitative results are generally convincing.

The architecture is conceptually simple and practical: compact tokens encode camera parameters, spatially aligned tokens encode depth, and stochastic prior dropout permits multiple input configurations without separate models.

The manuscript is well organized and visually clear. It also provides a candid limitations section acknowledging weak performance on dynamic/driving scenes, resolution constraints, and poor scaling to thousands of views.
weaknesses: Soundness is weakened by an important ambiguity about camera information in novel-view synthesis. Section 3 states that Gaussian centers are computed using ground-truth poses and intrinsics, while Table 6 separately ablates 'w/o GT Cameras'; this is difficult to reconcile with the claimed pose-free results and the no-prior rows in Table 4. The exact camera information used during training and evaluation must be specified, and headline comparisons should use matched camera access.

The description of Gaussian positioning is internally inconsistent. Section 3 and Appendix A say that a dedicated Gaussian head predicts Gaussian depth/positions rather than using the ordinary depth head, whereas the Table 6 discussion says positions are derived from the depth head. This prevents reliable interpretation or reproduction of the method.

Several comparisons do not adequately isolate the claimed contribution. The model starts from VGGT, trains on 15 datasets using 32 H20 GPUs, and adds data and tasks, but there is no controlled VGGT comparison matched for training data, compute, and fine-tuning. Likewise, the paper claims benefits from multi-task learning, curriculum learning, and dynamic prior injection without ablating these central components. The normal-estimation comparison also does not clearly state whether WorldMirror and the largely monocular baselines receive the same number of views.

The 'any-prior' evidence is too idealized. Experiments appear to use complete ground-truth depth, poses, and intrinsics. There are no tests with sparse, noisy, partially missing, miscalibrated, or real sensor priors, even though these conditions motivate the method. Feeding target-like ground-truth depth makes the large reconstruction improvements unsurprising.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the scale of the system. Code and models are only promised; the manuscript omits backbone/model size, precise dataset sampling ratios and splits, optimizer and regularization details, training steps or per-epoch definition, prior preprocessing and invalid-depth handling, view-sampling rules, random seeds, variance, and inference hardware. Randomly sampling 200 RealEstate10K scenes without publishing the sampled identities further hinders replication.

Some technical definitions need correction or clarification: depth normalization to [0,1] is underspecified and may discard metric scale; camera-scale normalization does not fully define the center or degenerate cases; and the absolute dot product in the normal loss treats opposite normal directions as equivalent despite evaluation typically using oriented normals.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Most components are direct extensions of VGGT with lightweight prior embeddings and additional task heads; the paper's novelty is primarily integration and scale. That can still be valuable, but the current ablations do not establish which integration choices are responsible for the gains.

The paper does not discuss dataset licenses, privacy implications of reconstructing captured environments, or misuse considerations. No acute ethical issue is evident, but a model trained across many real-world datasets should document data governance and privacy risks.

strengths: The paper tackles a useful problem: one feed-forward system accepts optional depth, intrinsics, and pose cues while producing point maps, depth, cameras, normals, and 3D Gaussians. This breadth could be practically valuable.

The empirical coverage is broad, spanning reconstruction, pose, normals, depth, and novel-view synthesis. The no-prior model reports competitive results, while several prior-conditioned configurations show substantial gains.
The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished. The token-based conditioning mechanism is simple, computationally lightweight, and easy to understand.
The limitations section honestly acknowledges weaknesses on dynamic/driving scenes, restricted resolution, and poor scaling to thousands of views.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central gains cannot be attributed convincingly to the proposed ideas. WorldMirror initializes from VGGT, trains on 15 datasets using 32 H20 GPUs, and adds several tasks, yet there is no controlled VGGT baseline with the same data, compute, resolution, and training recipe. Improvements may therefore arise from scale or data rather than prior prompting or unified prediction.

The claimed curriculum and multi-task benefits are essentially untested. There are no ablations for joint versus separate task training, task ordering, data scheduling, progressive resolution, or the effect of individual heads. The only architectural ablations cover prior encoding and parts of the Gaussian head.

Table 6 does not support the text's claim that every Gaussian component is crucial: replacing ground-truth cameras changes results only marginally and sometimes improves them; removing the GS DPT also improves VR-NeRF LPIPS. These mixed outcomes are presented as uniformly confirmatory.

The prior-guidance evaluation risks target leakage or trivialization. Supplying dense ground-truth depth when evaluating predicted depth and point geometry gives the model information closely related to the target. The paper does not evaluate sparse, noisy, biased, or estimated priors, despite real sensors and upstream predictors having these properties.

The claim of supporting arbitrary prior subsets is incompletely validated. Only selected configurations are reported, without systematic evaluation of all combinations, missing-view priors, conflicting priors, or graceful degradation as prior quality changes.

Several protocol details needed to interpret fairness are absent. In particular, the number of views used for normal estimation is unclear while comparisons are largely against single-image methods; geometric alignment and scaling procedures are insufficiently specified; and no variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-run results are provided.

The novel-view synthesis formulation is ambiguous about which cameras are used at inference. Section 3.2 back-projects Gaussian centers using ground-truth poses and intrinsics, while the paper also claims pose-free inference and Table 6 refers to predicted cameras. The exact train/test computation should be stated unambiguously.

Some geometric motivation is inaccurate or underspecified. Calibrated intrinsics alone do not resolve global metric scale; camera normalization refers ambiguously to a “camera center” while operating on extrinsic translations; per-map depth normalization to [0,1] is not defined and may discard metric scale; and quaternion sign conventions are omitted.

Originality is limited relative to VGGT and related prior-conditioned reconstruction systems: the main mechanism consists of MLP-projected global tokens, additive depth tokens, modality dropout, and additional DPT heads. The manuscript does not establish a sufficiently new technical principle beyond combining known components at larger scope.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Code and models are only promised, and the manuscript omits backbone dimensions and parameter count, dataset sampling weights, exact schedules and curriculum transitions, loss details and constants, candidate-split count, voxelization/pruning settings, evaluation preprocessing, and inference memory requirements.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: the model is described as trained end-to-end with a composite loss, but the Gaussian phase freezes all other parameters; the stated two-phase schedule conflicts with the later multi-stage task curriculum; and “universal” or “all-in-one” overstates a fixed set of five outputs with substantial scalability limitations.

Ethics and broader impacts receive no treatment. Given use of numerous aggregated datasets and generation of photorealistic novel views, the paper should at least document dataset licensing/consent considerations and discuss privacy or misuse risks. This is secondary to the technical concerns but remains a reproducibility and responsible-release omission.

strengths: Soundness/significance: The empirical scope is unusually broad. One feed-forward model is evaluated on point-map reconstruction, camera estimation, monocular/video depth, surface normals, and novel-view synthesis across many datasets. The reported gains are often substantial—for example, the no-prior model improves over VGGT on all reported point-map benchmarks, and it considerably exceeds AnySplat on the main NVS metrics.

The optional-prior interface is practically useful: camera poses, intrinsics, and depth can be supplied in arbitrary combinations, while random modality dropout allows the same model to operate without priors. Table 1 and Figure 6 provide consistent evidence that these inputs improve multiple geometric outputs rather than only their directly corresponding tasks.

The work integrates a broad set of outputs—point maps, depth, cameras, normals, and 3D Gaussians—within a coherent VGGT-style architecture. Although the individual components are mostly familiar, their combination constitutes a useful and ambitious systems contribution.

The evaluation covers sparse and dense NVS, scene- and object-level reconstruction, dynamic camera benchmarks, and held-out scenes. Qualitative results generally support the numerical trends, while the post-optimization experiment demonstrates a useful downstream benefit of the feed-forward initialization.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The manuscript gives losses, optimizer rates, loss weights, hardware, training phases, resolution ranges, and the 15-dataset training mixture. It also candidly identifies weaknesses on dynamic/driving data and scaling limitations for very long sequences; these are appropriate limitations rather than reasons by themselves to penalize the work.
No immediate severe research-ethics concern is apparent: the work concerns geometric reconstruction on established datasets, and its limitations are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: The NVS protocol has a consequential ambiguity. Section 3.2 says Gaussian centers are back-projected using ground-truth poses and intrinsics, and Table 6 defines “w/o GT Cameras” as replacing these quantities with predicted cameras. This implies that the main “WorldMirror” NVS results may use ground-truth cameras even in rows described as having no priors, which conflicts with the paper's pose-free framing and complicates comparison with uncalibrated methods such as AnySplat. The predicted-camera ablation remains strong, but the main tables must clearly distinguish calibrated from genuinely pose-free inference.

Several central design claims are insufficiently ablated. There is no controlled test of dynamic prior dropout, the three-part curriculum, joint multi-task learning versus separate heads/models, progressive resolution, or the claimed cross-output geometric consistency. Consequently, the results establish strong aggregate performance but do not establish that the proposed training mechanisms cause it.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. The backbone, alternating attention, DPT heads, point/depth/camera losses, Gaussian prediction, voxel pruning, and differentiable rendering substantially follow VGGT and prior NVS systems. Encoding compact camera information as tokens and depth as aligned dense features is sensible, but technically straightforward; the main novelty is breadth of integration.

Comparison and evaluation details leave fairness questions. Pow3R, the most directly related prior-conditioned reconstruction method discussed by the authors, is not evaluated. The number of input views for the surface-normal benchmarks is unspecified, making comparison with single-image normal estimators difficult to interpret. DL3DV is both part of the training collection and an NVS evaluation dataset, so describing that evaluation as “zero-shot” requires clarification at the dataset-versus-scene level.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for a large training effort. Code and models are only promised; the manuscript omits the exact backbone configuration and parameter count, dataset sampling weights, sample/view construction, invalid-depth handling and depth normalization procedure, pseudo-normal plane-fitting details, random seeds, variance over runs, and sufficient evaluation/alignment preprocessing. Epoch counts over a heterogeneous 15-dataset mixture do not uniquely specify the number of optimization steps.

Some mathematical and methodological descriptions need correction. The camera-pose normalization does not precisely define the center or coordinate convention; the camera output representation is underspecified; the normal loss uses an undefined weight and an absolute dot product that treats opposite orientations as equivalent; and the appendix inconsistently describes whether the normal head is present from the start. Known intrinsics also do not generally resolve absolute scene scale as claimed.

The efficiency claim is weakly supported. Feed-forward times are reported only coarsely as under two seconds, without matched hardware, model size, memory consumption, throughput versus input-view count, or comparisons under equal resolution. Given the stated requirement of 32 H20 GPUs for training and inability to handle thousands of views, a more complete computational analysis is important.

The limitations section covers domain gaps and scalability but omits other important issues: sensitivity to noisy or inconsistent priors, partial/sparse depth, erroneous calibration, uncertainty calibration, dataset licensing and governance for the aggregated training corpus, and possible privacy or surveillance implications of reconstructing real environments. These omissions are not evidence of misconduct, but should be addressed.

strengths: Soundness: The paper evaluates a broad set of outputs—point maps, cameras, depth, normals, and 3D Gaussians—across numerous datasets. The no-prior model is competitive with strong feed-forward baselines, and the appendix includes useful robustness, memory, latency, training-strategy, and prior-dropout studies.

Significance: A single model that accepts optional poses, intrinsics, and depth while producing several complementary 3D representations would be practically useful. The reported gains are substantial in several settings, including point reconstruction with all priors and dense-view novel-view synthesis.

Presentation: The overall architecture and staged training rationale are easy to follow, and the main tables and qualitative figures communicate the intended capabilities clearly. The limitations section appropriately identifies weaknesses on dynamic/driving data and scaling to very long sequences.

Originality: Combining flexible prior conditioning with geometry, normal, camera, and Gaussian prediction in one system is a useful synthesis, even though the individual mechanisms are largely established.

Reproducibility and ethics: The appendix reports datasets, loss weights, learning rates, hardware, training time, resolutions, memory, and inference speed. The impact statement acknowledges privacy, misrepresentation, and bias risks without overstating mitigation. weaknesses: Soundness: The central attribution to the proposed unified design is not established. WorldMirror is initialized from VGGT and trained on 15 heterogeneous datasets, while competing models have different data, objectives, and capacities. The paper itself attributes NVS gains partly to broader training data, but provides no matched-data, matched-compute comparison against VGGT plus equivalent heads or prior adapters.

The claim that priors yield “universal gains across all tasks” is contradicted by the reported results. In Table 1, pose conditioning worsens DTU completeness relative to the no-prior model; in Table 12, clean depth worsens both 7-Scenes metrics and clean intrinsics worsens 7-Scenes accuracy; Figure 7 also does not show every prior improving every metric. These discrepancies require a narrower claim and explanation.

Several evaluation protocols are insufficiently specified for fair interpretation. Table 3 does not state whether WorldMirror receives one or multiple views when compared with single-image normal estimators. NVS tables use different resolutions, pose alignment/optimization, and prior conditions, and Tables 4 and 9 report markedly different DL3DV numbers without enough protocol detail to reconcile them. No confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are reported.

The appearance pipeline is ambiguous at a central point: the method says Gaussian positions use predicted depth and ground-truth cameras, while the system is advertised as pose-free at inference. It is unclear exactly when ground-truth versus predicted cameras are used during training, Gaussian construction, rendering supervision, and evaluation. Table 6 does not fully resolve this ambiguity.

Originality is limited at the component level: concatenating global pose/intrinsic tokens, adding dense depth embeddings, attaching DPT task heads, and freezing geometry before training a Gaussian head are straightforward extensions of VGGT and prior-guided reconstruction. The paper does not convincingly distinguish its conceptual contribution from closely related MapAnything and OmniVGGT beyond output coverage and fusion details.

The ablations do not isolate several major claims. There is no controlled test of whether multi-task prediction improves each task over separately trained or geometry-only counterparts, and the staged-training comparison changes optimization structure without analyzing which task conflicts matter. Table 6 shows some ablations matching or improving individual metrics, weakening the assertion that every proposed NVS component is essential.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix: model size and backbone configuration, token dimension, decoder details, dataset sampling ratios, augmentation and preprocessing rules, view-sampling policy, optimizer/batch details, and precise evaluation/alignment procedures are missing or incomplete. The manuscript states that code and weights are public, but supplies no accessible link in the reviewed version. The normal loss also uses an absolute dot product, making flipped normals equivalent, without discussing compatibility with the oriented-normal evaluation.

Presentation contains consequential imprecision, including an equation describing the predicted normal as a camera variable, inconsistent descriptions of two versus three training stages, and unexplained numerical inconsistencies across tables. The ethics discussion is appropriate but generic and offers no concrete privacy or misuse safeguards. Overall, the promising breadth does not yet outweigh the attribution, protocol, and reproducibility gaps.

strengths: Significance: A single feed-forward interface that accepts optional poses, intrinsics, and depth while predicting cameras, point maps, depth, normals, and 3D Gaussians would be practically useful. The paper evaluates an unusually broad range of 3D tasks and reports latency and memory scaling.

Soundness: The empirical results are often strong, particularly for point-map reconstruction and surface-normal estimation. The appendix adds useful experiments on prior dropout, noisy priors, depth injection, curriculum training, view-count scaling, and post-optimization.

The compact-token treatment of global camera information and additive fusion of dense depth are simple, computationally motivated design choices. Table 5 provides some evidence that compact tokens can outperform denser pose/intrinsic encodings with fewer parameters.

Presentation: The main architecture and training stages are generally easy to follow, and the figures are visually informative. Table 13 offers a controlled joint-versus-decoupled training comparison rather than relying entirely on comparisons with external systems.

The paper reports important practical details, including loss weights, learning rates, GPU count, wall-clock training time, inference latency, and memory consumption. It also includes limitations and an impact statement acknowledging privacy, misrepresentation, and bias risks.
weaknesses: Soundness: The experiments do not isolate the cause of the reported gains. WorldMirror is initialized from VGGT and trained on 15 datasets, while compared methods differ substantially in architecture, training data, supervision, and resolution. The paper itself attributes novel-view gains partly to broader training data. There is no controlled VGGT baseline retrained on the same data, nor a factorial ablation separating data scale, prior tokenization, normal supervision, multitask learning, and the Gaussian head. Consequently, the central claim that the unified design produces the improvements is not established.

Several results contradict the claimed universal benefit of priors. In Table 12, clean depth worsens 7-Scenes accuracy from 0.044 to 0.058, clean intrinsics worsens it to 0.047, and clean pose worsens DTU completeness from 1.486 to 1.502. These values also disagree materially with the corresponding configurations in Table 1, without an explanation of protocol or checkpoint differences.

The novel-view evidence is overstated and not consistently favorable. Against AnySplat without priors in Table 4, WorldMirror has worse LPIPS at 24 and 64 views. Table 6 also gives nearly identical RealEstate10K results with and without ground-truth cameras, and removing the proposed GS DPT improves VR-NeRF LPIPS. These mixed results do not support the claim that every listed component is essential. Comparisons additionally mix resolutions, prior availability, pose-free optimization, and test-time camera alignment, making fairness difficult to assess.

Important methodological details are unclear. The appearance model says Gaussian positions are computed using predicted depth and ground-truth cameras, but the exact pose-free inference path is not specified. Depth normalization to [0,1] lacks a precise definition. The paper does not adequately specify dataset sampling ratios, preprocessing, split hygiene, metric alignment, or units. In particular, claiming that intrinsics resolve scale ambiguity is geometrically incorrect: calibrated intrinsics resolve focal-length ambiguity but do not determine global scene scale.

The normal loss uses an absolute dot product, making opposite normal directions equivalent, while the reported angular metrics and downstream surface reconstruction normally require consistently oriented normals. The manuscript does not explain this mismatch or report orientation failures.

Originality: Most ingredients are direct extensions of VGGT—small modality tokenizers, additional DPT heads, a Gaussian head, modality dropout, and staged freezing. Closely related Pow3R, MapAnything, and OmniVGGT already condition reconstruction on geometric priors. The distinction is mainly combining existing capabilities and outputs, and the paper does not convincingly demonstrate new principles beyond this integration.

Significance is reduced by the meaning of “any-prior”: only three dense, fully available geometric priors are supported. Sparse or partial depth, uncertain calibration, inconsistent subsets of views, and real sensor failures are not studied. Synthetic noise experiments are useful but do not validate robust operation with naturally imperfect priors.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the useful compute details. The abstract states that code and weights are publicly available, but the location is blank, and the manuscript does not provide enough architecture, data-mixture, preprocessing, or evaluation detail to independently reproduce the results. The enormous 32-H20 training setup also makes independent verification difficult.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: Appendix C.2 says “depth and normal priors” are dropped even though normals are not an input prior; the paper alternates between two-phase and apparently three-step training descriptions; it calls the system end-to-end although the Gaussian stage freezes the rest of the model; and the limitation that it cannot handle view counts “into the thousands” sits awkwardly beside the claimed 1,024-view capacity. The limitations and ethics discussions are present but generic and omit dependence on potentially privacy-sensitive aggregated training datasets and failure risks from confidently incorrect geometry.

strengths: WorldMirror offers a useful unified system: one VGGT-based model accepts optional pose, intrinsic, and depth priors and predicts cameras, point maps, depth, normals, and 3D Gaussians. Combining flexible conditioning with broad output coverage is practically significant, even though the individual mechanisms are mostly extensions of established components. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/e595d0cdad424442884716f1f48f932b/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation is unusually broad. The paper reports strong results across point-map reconstruction, camera estimation, monocular/video depth, surface normals, and novel-view synthesis. Particularly convincing results include the large reconstruction gains from combining all priors in Table 1, improvements over VGGT on several no-prior benchmarks, and substantial NVS gains over AnySplat in Table 9.

The authors include several valuable diagnostic experiments: comparisons to prior-guided methods, alternative prior embeddings, prior-dropout sensitivity, noisy-prior robustness, joint versus sequential training, multi-view scaling, memory use, inference latency, and wall-clock training cost. These materially improve the empirical case and expose important tradeoffs.

The compact global-token treatment of poses and intrinsics is simple and efficient. Table 5 indicates that it is competitive with denser Plücker/ray-map encodings while using substantially fewer additional parameters. The modular, on-demand 3DGS head and approximately 13% full-model overhead at 64 views also make the system practically attractive.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, with helpful architectural and qualitative figures. It also discusses limitations involving dynamic/driving scenes, resolution, long sequences, and consumer-GPU memory rather than concealing them.
The impact statement appropriately identifies privacy, environmental misrepresentation, and bias risks. No unresolved ethical issue appears to preclude publication.
weaknesses: The strongest claim—that prior injection provides universal gains across all tasks—is not supported literally by the reported evidence. In Table 12, even clean depth worsens 7-Scenes accuracy from 0.044 to 0.058, clean intrinsics worsen it to 0.047, and clean pose slightly worsens DTU completeness. Table 1 also contains unchanged or degraded metrics for individual priors. The claim should be weakened to gains in most settings and accompanied by an analysis of harmful-prior cases.

Some headline comparisons are insufficiently controlled. The authors acknowledge that NVS gains partly reflect broader training data, while the method is initialized from VGGT and trained on 15 datasets. There is no data-matched comparison that isolates the unified architecture from initialization and training-scale effects. Likewise, Table 3 compares against specialized surface-normal methods without clearly stating whether WorldMirror uses the same single-view input protocol; a multi-view versus monocular comparison would not substantiate the claimed superiority.

The 3DGS ablation provides weak support for the claim that every design choice is essential. In Table 6, several differences are tiny, and ablations sometimes outperform the full model—for example, “w/o GT Cameras” has slightly higher RealEstate10K PSNR, “w/o Novel Views” has better DL3DV LPIPS, and “w/o GS DPT” has better VR-NeRF LPIPS. No repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance analysis are provided.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous despite the extensive appendix. The description alternately says Gaussian positions are computed from predicted depth and ground-truth cameras and that the GS head predicts positions independently; the precise pose-free inference path is not fully specified. The total architecture size, dataset sampling ratios, exact train/test filtering, candidate-split count K, preprocessing details, and some loss definitions are also missing or unclear. The manuscript as supplied says code and weights are public but provides no URL, limiting current reproducibility.

The normal loss uses an absolute dot product, making opposite normal directions equivalent, without explaining why this is compatible with the oriented angular evaluation. Other presentation inconsistencies include referring to the supervised normal as E rather than N and Appendix C.2 saying that “depth and normal priors” are dropped even though normals are not an input prior. These do not invalidate the results but reduce technical precision.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. The backbone and several prediction heads closely follow VGGT; token conditioning, modality dropout, DPT heads, staged training, and 3DGS supervision are familiar ideas. Concurrent systems such as MapAnything and OmniVGGT already address heterogeneous prior injection. The contribution is therefore chiefly the effective integration and broad evaluation of these elements.

The limitations discussion is useful but omits dependence on expensive supervision and 32 H20 GPUs, sensitivity to incorrect priors beyond synthetic perturbations, and possible dataset-license or privacy considerations arising from aggregation of 15 datasets. These should be documented more concretely for reproducible and responsible deployment.
